name: Tsunami
label: Simple Machines
lede: Two housemates who ran a record label from their living room started a band for a New Year's party and toured it for seven years.

eras.title: A New Year's party that never ended
eras.text: Two housemates in a Positive Force activist house in Arlington, Virginia, who already ran a label out of their living space, start a band for a party. Their first tour opens for Beat Happening within weeks.

years.h: [[Jenny Toomey|246fc8dd-a667-4a5b-868a-a5897bcd6c59]] and [[Kristin Thomson|a7a793e4-d41c-4286-a494-03a31305b4bc]] form Tsunami in an Arlington house
years.p: The Simple Machines co-founders recruit drummer John Pamer and bassist Andrew Webster from Bricks. Wikipedia says the band began to play a New Year's party.
years.xp:
Toomey and Thomson were housemates in an Arlington communal house tied to the activist group Positive Force, and they were already running Simple Machines from it. Washingtonian describes the house as the band's birthplace.

Tsunami's own bio says the first show came in January 1991, before there was a real batch of songs to play.

years.h: First show, before the songs exist
years.p: Tsunami's bio says the band played its first show in January 1991, ahead of any real songwriting.

years.h: First tour: opening for Beat Happening
years.p: Weeks after that first show, Tsunami went on the road as support for [[Beat Happening|449e44cb-bcae-4c48-a1af-5d8df0f81456]], according to the band's bio.

years.h: Olympia and the fleas: the International Pop Underground festival
years.p: Tsunami played the Olympia festival that also had [[Bikini Kill|1397d045-1603-41fc-80b9-712c18360145]], [[Fugazi|233fc3f3-6de2-465c-985e-e721dbabbace]] and Thee Headcoats, weeks before Nevermind arrived.
years.xp:
Toomey told WNYU's Static the band slept in a tent set up in the aisle of the Capitol Theater because of the fleas. The trip fed straight back into DC.

Eight weeks after coming home, Simple Machines put on its own festival.

years.h: Lots of Pop Losers: fourteen bands, two days, no internet
years.p: Simple Machines organized the DC festival about eight weeks after returning from Olympia, booking 14 bands by mail and phone.
years.xp: Toomey described the pre-internet logistics to WNYU's Static. The festival was a Simple Machines project, with Tsunami among the acts.

eras.title: Seven-inches, Lollapalooza and 150 shows
eras.text: A stack of singles, a debut album held up by the pressing plant, and a year on the road that also fed a record club and a second album.

years.h: Split single with [[Velocity Girl|b199e343-e7f2-4840-8111-6cdb62945025]] on Sub Pop
years.p: One of the first Tsunami singles to travel beyond the Simple Machines catalog, paired with Maryland's Velocity Girl.
years.xp: Wikipedia lists the 7-inch on Sub Pop, 1992, among a run of singles the band put out before its debut album.

years.h: Deep End is recorded, then sits in the pipeline
years.p: The band recorded its debut album in summer 1992; manufacturing and mixing delays pushed release into early 1993.

years.h: Deep End: the debut, on Simple Machines
years.p: Tsunami's first album arrived after a run of seven-inches, with interlocking guitars and two singing bandleaders.
years.xp: The Washington Post and the band's own press pages describe the sound as a mix of math rock, Riot Grrrl and a touch of twee, built on DIY habits.

years.h: Six Lollapalooza side-stage shows with Sebadoh and Free Kitten
years.p: Tsunami took the festival's side stage alongside [[Sebadoh|d98c8149-0c01-4151-93e1-48fdc3d5027f]], [[Free Kitten|7e623dd5-bf40-4f8b-ba71-8226afc918e2]] and [[Thurston Moore|8ba48525-d922-42ee-9775-97b7b8f9712e]].
years.xp:
Toomey told WNYU's Static that 1993 meant Lollapalooza dates plus roughly 150 other shows. The band was also recording its second album while touring.

Back at the label, Simple Machines was running its Working Holiday record club, which had about 800 members.

years.h: The Heart's Tremolo: album two, written on the road
years.p: The second album was recorded while the band toured hard; two US tours, an English tour and a Phoenix Festival slot on the Melody Maker stage followed.
years.xp: Wikipedia counts two US tours and one England tour after the record, with the Phoenix Festival appearance on the Melody Maker Stage.

years.h: Working Holiday! compilation on Simple Machines
years.p: Tsunami contributed to the label's Working Holiday! compilation, tied to the record club.

eras.title: A drummer goes to college
eras.text: Tsunami keeps releasing singles while the founding rhythm section unwinds. A split with Superchunk's label and a new drummer set up the last album.

years.h: World Tour & Other Destinations, a collection of singles
years.p: Compiles the band's run of 7-inch releases; Wikipedia lists it as a Simple Machines release.

years.h: Split single with [[Superchunk|61653550-fd9b-4401-8248-44f2d064d384]] on Merge's Honeybear
years.p: Tsunami and Superchunk shared a 7-inch, Wikipedia says on Honeybear, in 1995.

years.h: John Pamer leaves for UMass Amherst for a year
years.p: The drummer took a one-year hiatus to study at UMass Amherst, per Wikipedia.

years.h: Luther Gray takes the drums; Webster and Pamer are out
years.p: Pamer graduated and stayed in Amherst, then moved on to New York City. Arlington drummer Luther Gray stepped in.
years.xp: Tsunami's bio dates the departures of Andrew Webster and John Pamer to 1996. Gray was an Arlington drummer.

eras.title: A Brilliant Mistake, then the lights go off
eras.text: The last album is made in Chicago with a bigger lineup, and in 1998 Toomey and Thomson close both the label and the band.

years.h: A Brilliant Mistake, cut at Kingsize Soundlabs in Chicago
years.p: Recorded with Luther Gray on drums, it added cellist-bassist Amy Domingues and guitarist-keyboardist Bob Massey for the tour.
years.xp: Wikipedia says Domingues and Massey joined on the tour for the album. The band credits the album as its third full-length after Deep End and The Heart's Tremolo.

years.h: Amy Domingues and Bob Massey join for the last tour
years.p: Domingues plays bass and cello, Massey guitar and keyboards.

years.h: The Simple Machines Finale party
years.p: Toomey and Thomson closed Simple Machines, which had put out nearly 80 releases, and played the finale with Tsunami.
years.xp:
The band's bio dates the party to March 1998, after which it ceased regular activity. Wikipedia says the two closed the label and disbanded Tsunami that year after a final East Coast tour.

The label's Mechanics Guide to Putting Out Records had spread its know-how to hundreds of would-be label owners, including future Numero Group co-founder Ken Shipley.

eras.title: Ladyfests and the Future of Music
eras.text: The members turn the label's ethic into policy work, and the band turns up only for special occasions.

years.h: Toomey and Thomson co-found the Future of Music Coalition
years.p: After Simple Machines, Toomey became executive director and Thomson education director of the advocacy group, says Wikipedia. The Creative Independent notes Tsunami also played a handful of shows in 2000.

years.h: Ladyfest sets in Washington and Philadelphia
years.p: Between 2001 and 2003 Toomey and Thomson played two Ladyfest sets with former members and guests, in DC and Philadelphia.

eras.title: Loud Is As
eras.text: Numero Group digs the band out of the archive, and Tsunami, with a new rhythm section, goes back on the road.

years.h: Reunited at Numero Twenty in Los Angeles
years.p: The band's bio says it reformed for the Numero Group festival, alongside the label's reissue project.
years.xp: The current lineup is Toomey and Thomson, Luther Gray, Rob Christiansen on bass and Franklin Bruno on guitar and keyboards.

years.src: Washingtonian · The Big Takeover · Wikipedia · WNYU Static interview
years.h: Loud Is As: five LPs, every album, every single
years.p: Numero Group's box set has 61 songs, 1991 demos and a book of essays and photos; The Big Takeover called it a marvel of physical preservation.
years.xp:
Washingtonian gives a release date of November 8, 2024; the Inquirer says October. Thomson and Toomey told WNYU's Static they used only about 2 percent of their archive of journals, letters and flyers.

Wikipedia reports it appeared on best-of lists at the New York Times and Billboard and was nominated for a Grammy for Best Recording Package at the 2026 awards.

years.h: The Coin Toss Tour with [[Ida|19c960a1-703e-48e4-8286-37b3aee7a09c]]
years.p: A coin flip each night decided who opened, Tsunami or Ida; a DC hometown show at the Black Cat was announced for March 27, and Philadelphia's Underground Arts followed on March 28.
years.xp: Washingtonian announced the Black Cat date and the Inquirer described the Philadelphia stop; they list each as the tour's first show, so the opening night is unclear.
